primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- how a Dissent became the ponencia in Phimco Industries v. Brillantes, offered as an illustration that justices do change their minds when persuaded by reasoned argument before promulgation.

The holding that the labor secretary gravely abused his discretion by assuming jurisdiction over a strike at a match factory on the basis of "obtaining circumstances" rather than a finding that the industry is indispensable to the national interest.

CJP's survey of the jurisprudence on Article 263 (g): the cases in which assumption was allowed (schools, a large exporter, drugs and pharmaceuticals, a domestic airline, a major tire producer) against those in which it was disallowed, most eloquently GTE Directories.

The historical argument that the power to restrict strikes is of martial law vintage, that even General Order No. 5 listed the vital industries it covered, and that after Republic Act 6715 the secretary's undefined discretion remains subject to judicial review.
The police-power reading of assumption of jurisdiction -- justified only by public necessity -- and the observation that state intervention is not always beneficial to labor.
sub_topics: The opening reflection that during internal deliberations justices argue logically and sometimes passionately but are not bigots or stubborn of heart, and may change their votes at any time before promulgation, or even after, on a motion for reconsideration.

The facts of Phimco: PILA's Notice of Strike of March 9, 1995 filed with the National Conciliation and Mediation Board after a deadlocked negotiation, the strike by its 352 members, the acting secretary's assumption of jurisdiction and return-to-work order of July 7, 1995 at PILA's own petition, and Phimco's challenge for grave abuse of discretion.
Justice Purisima's initial recommendation to dismiss the petition on the view that the secretary had the prerogative to take over a dispute imbued with national interest.

CJP's Dissent contending that a match factory could hardly be indispensable to the national interest, and his success in convincing the whole Third Division -- including Purisima, who changed his mind and wrote the contrary ponencia.

The revised ponencia's reasoning that grounding assumption on obtaining circumstances rather than the legislated standard would let the secretary intervene in any dispute at his pleasure, and that an overzealous official who by-passes the law makes the law lose its meaning.
The Division's request that CJP convert his Dissent into a Concurring Opinion, quoted in toto.
The text of Article 263 (g) quoted in full, including the automatic injunction, the return-to-work and readmission duties, and the President's separate power to determine indispensable industries.

The conclusion from the text that assumption is meant to be used sparingly and only if the national interest demands it, and that the secretary must respect labor's paramount right to concerted activities.

The cases where national interest was found: school administration in Philippine School of Business Administration v. Noriel; a firm exporting 90 percent of production and earning over $12 million a year in Sarmiento v. Tuico; drugs and pharmaceuticals; a domestic airline; and a company responsible for 22 percent of Philippine tire production.

GTE Directories Corporation v. Sanchez, where a telephone-directory publisher was held not to be an industry affecting the national interest, its revenues coming chiefly from advertising space and its role in communication not comparable to mass media.

The breadth of the powers that follow assumption, illustrated by The Philippine American Management Co. v. PAMEA-FFW, including jurisdiction over all incidents to avoid diametrically opposed rulings, and the forfeiture of employment for defying a return-to-work order.

The martial law precursor: Proclamation No. 1081, General Order No. 5 prohibiting strikes and picketing in vital industries, and Letter of Instructions No. 368 enumerating those industries in detail -- public utilities, essential commodities, exporters, mining, banking, government infrastructure, hospitals and schools.

The point that even at the height of martial rule there was no blanket authority to assume jurisdiction without a showing of national interest, national security or general welfare, and that RA 6715 left the secretary discretion that is nonetheless reviewable.

The police power argument: a prolonged strike can be inimical to the national economy, but public necessity and self-protection are absent where the industry is not indispensable, and free enterprise favors letting labor negotiate without government intervention.

The argument that intervention is not always beneficial to labor, more often favoring management which avoids overhead wasted during a work stoppage, and that other remedies -- illegal dismissal cases, dismissal of illegal strikers, negotiation -- remain available.

The secretary's own admission that the case did not on its face fall within the strict categorization of national interest, his rationalization from prolonged work disruption and community jeopardy, and the rebuttal that Phimco's exports were negligible under the Omnibus Rules definition.

The peculiarity that it was the union rather than management that petitioned for assumption, having apparently lost belief in its own strike, while the employer objected because it was unwilling to readmit all the strikers -- so that the assumption merely muddled the issues.

The closing judgment that the secretary's intention to reconcile the disputants may have been noble but does not imbue a dispute with national interest, and the epilogue that a case begun as a battle ended as a victory for all.

stances.claim: A labor dispute must seriously and deleteriously affect an industry indispensable to the national interest before the secretary may assume jurisdiction over it; a match factory is not such an industry.
stances.rhetorical_move: statutory-standard argument: holding the official to the legislated criterion he himself admitted was not met

stances.claim: Assumption of jurisdiction is meant to be used sparingly, since the secretary, like everyone else, must respect labor's paramount right to stage concerted activities.
stances.rhetorical_move: reading the text and tenor of Article 263 (g) as an exception to a right rather than a general power

stances.claim: The almost unlimited breadth of the powers that follow assumption calls for caution in the official who holds them and strict scrutiny of government excess by the judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: power-proportionate-scrutiny principle, stated after cataloguing how broad those powers are

stances.claim: Even at the height of martial rule there was no blanket authority to ban strikes: General Order No. 5 rested on a stated public purpose and an enumerated list of vital industries, so today's undefined discretion cannot be greater.
stances.rhetorical_move: a fortiori historical argument drawn from the martial law issuances quoted at length

stances.claim: Government intervention is not always beneficial to labor; more often it advantages management, which avoids overhead otherwise wasted during a work stoppage, and other remedies remain available to both sides.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the protective rationale against itself by tracing who actually gains from a return-to-work order

stances.claim: The secretary's noble intention to reconcile the disputants does not imbue the dispute with national interest or clothe him with power to assume jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: proverbial dismissal -- the road to damnation paved with good intentions -- separating motive from authority

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' used Phimco Industries v. Brillantes to show that justices do change their minds when persuaded, since practice allows a vote to change at any time before promulgation. Justice Panganiban recounted the facts: after a deadlocked collective bargaining negotiation, the Phimco Industries Labor Association filed a Notice of Strike in March 1995 and its 352 members struck; at the union's own petition the acting Secretary of Labor assumed jurisdiction in July and ordered the strikers back to work within 24 hours; and the match manufacturer challenged the order as grave abuse of discretion. Justice Purisima, to whom the case was assigned, first recommended dismissing the petition, but CJP's Dissent -- arguing that a match factory could hardly be indispensable to the national interest -- convinced the whole Third Division, and Purisima, in what CJP called a gallant show of humility, changed his mind and wrote the contrary ponencia, holding that grounding assumption on obtaining circumstances rather than the legislated standard would let the secretary intervene in any dispute at his pleasure. Asked by his colleagues to convert the Dissent into a Concurring Opinion, CJP reproduced it in full. He quoted Article 263 (g), concluded that assumption is meant to be used sparingly and that the secretary must respect labor's paramount right to concerted activities, and surveyed the cases: national interest had been found in school administration, a major exporter, drugs and pharmaceuticals, a domestic airline and a large tire producer, but denied most eloquently in GTE Directories, involving a telephone-directory publisher. He catalogued the broad powers that follow assumption and argued that their breadth calls for caution and strict judicial scrutiny. Tracing the power to its martial law vintage in General Order No. 5 and Letter of Instructions No. 368, which enumerated the vital industries covered, he observed that even then no blanket authority existed. He read Article 263 (g) as police power requiring public necessity, noted that intervention often favors management rather than labor, and rebutted the secretary's rationale, pointing out that Phimco's exports were negligible and that the secretary himself had admitted the case fell outside the strict categorization. Noble intentions, he concluded, do not confer jurisdiction; the case began as a battle but ended in a unanimous vote.
